drills.q: State the RNN hidden-state update equation and explain why it forces sequential (non-parallel) computation during training.
drills.a: h_t = tanh(W_hh h_{t-1} + W_xh x_t + b). Computing h_t requires h_{t-1} to already be computed, so step t cannot start until step t-1 finishes -- there is no way to compute all h_t values for a sequence in a single parallel batched operation the way attention can, because each depends on the previous one's output value, not just its existence in the computation graph.

drills.q: A vanilla RNN needs to connect information from position 1 to position 50 in a sequence. How many sequential recurrent steps does that require, and what does this imply about gradient magnitude in the worst case?
drills.a: 49 sequential steps. In the worst case, the gradient connecting those two positions is a product of 49 Jacobians dominated by W_hh and the activation derivative (max 1.0 for tanh, decaying elsewhere) -- if that per-step factor is consistently below 1, the compounded gradient after 49 multiplications can be vanishingly small, which is why vanilla RNNs struggle past roughly 10-20 step dependencies in practice.

drills.q: Derive why the LSTM cell-state update is described as an 'additive' gradient highway, contrasting it explicitly with the vanilla RNN's multiplicative update.
drills.a: Vanilla RNN: h_t = tanh(W_hh h_{t-1} + ...), so dh_t/dh_{t-1} involves W_hh and tanh'(*) multiplied together at every step -- a genuinely multiplicative chain. LSTM: c_t = f_t * c_{t-1} + i_t * g_t, so dc_t/dc_{t-1} = f_t (plus a smaller term from i_t*g_t's dependence on c_{t-1} through the gates, typically minor). When f_t is learned to be close to 1, this derivative is close to 1 regardless of depth, unlike the RNN case where the effective per-step factor is baked into W_hh and doesn't adapt.

drills.q: Explain what each of the four LSTM components (forget, input, candidate, output) computes and why the candidate uses tanh while the gates use sigmoid.
drills.a: Forget gate f_t = sigmoid(...): fraction of c_{t-1} to keep. Input gate i_t = sigmoid(...): fraction of new info to write. Candidate g_t = tanh(...): the actual new content, needs a signed range (-1,1) so it can add to or subtract from the cell state. Output gate o_t = sigmoid(...): fraction of c_t to expose as h_t. Gates use sigmoid because they represent a 0-1 fraction (how much to let through); the candidate uses tanh because it needs to be able to push the cell state up or down, requiring a signed value.

drills.q: You're choosing between LSTM and GRU for a resource-constrained edge deployment at hidden size 128. Estimate the relative parameter savings of GRU and explain the structural reason.
drills.a: GRU has 3 gate weight sets (update, reset, candidate) versus LSTM's 4 (forget, input, candidate, output), each roughly the same size at a given hidden size, so GRU uses about 3/4 = 75% of LSTM's gate parameters, i.e. roughly 25% fewer. The structural reason: GRU merges LSTM's forget and input gates into one update gate and eliminates the separate cell-state vector, folding long-term memory into the hidden state itself.

drills.q: A transformer's attention score matrix at sequence length n=8,192 with fp16 precision is roughly how large per head, and why does this become the practical bottleneck rather than the O(n^2) FLOP count itself?
drills.a: n^2 * 2 bytes = 8192^2 * 2 ~= 134MB per head. Memory becomes the practical bottleneck before compute because materializing that full matrix in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for every head, every layer, exceeds typical GPU memory budgets well before the FLOP count itself becomes infeasible on modern accelerators -- this is exactly what FlashAttention addresses via tiling, without changing the O(n^2) FLOP count.

drills.q: You need to deploy a keyword-spotting model on a microcontroller with 256KB RAM, processing a continuous, unbounded audio stream. Justify why neither a transformer nor a large 1D CNN is the right architecture, and what is.
drills.a: A transformer's KV cache grows linearly with how much of the stream has been processed, which is incompatible with an unbounded stream and a fixed tiny memory budget -- there's no natural point to cap context without losing detection ability. A large 1D CNN has a fixed receptive field, so while its per-step cost doesn't grow, it also can't accumulate state across the stream beyond that window, and the model itself may not fit the memory budget if using many layers/channels. A small LSTM or GRU is the right choice: its state is a small, constant-size vector updated one frame at a time, independent of how long the stream has been running.

drills.q: Explain the difference between a classical (S4-era) state-space model and Mamba's 'selective' state-space model.
drills.a: Classical SSMs have fixed transition parameters (the discretized linear dynamical system's matrices) regardless of the input content, so they process every position with the same fixed dynamics and can't dynamically decide what to remember or discard. Mamba makes the step size and transition matrices functions of the current input token, letting the model selectively prioritize or deprioritize information based on content -- conceptually similar to LSTM gating, but built on a state-space formulation with a parallel-scan algorithm that keeps training efficient despite the input-dependent recurrence.

drills.q: A colleague claims Mamba has already replaced transformers for large language models as of 2026. How would you correct this, precisely?
drills.a: Overstated. Mamba and other selective state-space models are a real, actively developed direction with strong reported results on specific benchmarks (language, genomics, sequences up to ~1M tokens on some tasks) and a genuine linear-time/constant-memory-per-step advantage over O(n^2) attention. But as of 2026, pure SSMs have not displaced transformers as the default for frontier general-purpose LLMs, and a meaningful share of current research builds hybrids interleaving attention and SSM layers rather than committing to either exclusively -- this is unresolved, not settled.

drills.q: Design the architecture selection reasoning (not just the answer) for a genomics model that needs to process sequences of up to 1 million base pairs to find long-range regulatory interactions.
drills.a: A vanilla or gated RNN would need ~1M sequential steps, making training painfully slow and gradient flow to distant positions unreliable even with LSTM gating at that scale. A standard transformer's O(n^2) attention at n=1,000,000 is computationally infeasible to materialize even with FlashAttention's memory savings, since the FLOP count itself is still quadratic. A 1D CNN has a fixed receptive field that would need enormous dilation/depth to reach 1M-length range and still wouldn't offer content-dependent, dynamic long-range weighting. This is exactly the regime where a selective state-space model (Mamba) is the strongest fit: linear-time, constant-memory-per-step scaling with input-dependent selectivity, and it has reported demonstrated benefits at sequence lengths around 1M tokens on some tasks -- while flagging that this is a less mature, less battle-tested choice than a transformer would be at more moderate lengths.

drills.q: Explain why an LSTM's constant per-step inference cost is actually a meaningfully different cost profile from a transformer's decode-time cost, even ignoring training-time parallelism entirely.
drills.a: An LSTM's per-step decode cost is O(1) regardless of how many tokens have already been generated or seen, because its state is a fixed-size vector. A transformer's per-step decode cost grows with context length: even with a KV cache avoiding recomputation, each new token's attention must still compute scores against every cached previous key, so decode cost per step grows linearly with sequence length so far (and the KV cache's memory footprint also grows linearly), unlike the RNN's genuinely flat cost.
